evidence.label: Symplectic Ball Packings in Higher Dimensions

headline: Proves Siegel and Yao's conjecture: from dimension six, ball packings are limited only by volume and the two-ball test.
scope: Finitely many closed standard symplectic balls of any positive capacities, packed into the interior of one ball, in real dimension 2n with n ≥ 3.
plain: A symplectic embedding moves a shape while keeping a special kind of area, not just volume. Gromov found that two balls can fail to fit in a bigger ball even when their volumes are small enough. Siegel and Yao conjectured that, from dimension six up, volume and Gromov's two-ball test are the only limits. This paper proves that conjecture for any number of balls of any sizes. Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal statements of this criterion.
doesNot: This does not cover dimension four, where extra obstructions are known to matter. It also does not give an explicit formula for the embeddings.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Mikhail Gromov, whose two-ball obstruction started symplectic packing rigidity
scorecard.significanceWhy: It gives, with Lean statements, a complete packing criterion for balls in all dimensions from six up, settling a conjecture of Siegel and Yao.

explanation:
Take a six-dimensional ball of capacity 1, the target. Capacity is π times the squared radius. Try to fit two smaller balls of capacity 0.6 inside it. Their volumes compare as cubes in six dimensions, so together they need 2 × 0.6³ = 0.432 of the target's volume. By volume alone they fit. But a symplectic map must keep a special kind of area, not just volume. Under that rule, two balls fit only if their capacities add to less than 1. Here 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2, so they do not fit. Now try eight balls of capacity 0.49. Each pair adds to 0.98, below 1. The volumes add to 8 × 0.49³, about 0.941. The paper says these eight balls do fit, filling about 94% of the volume. Nine such balls would need about 1.059, too much.

The setting is a symplectic space, a space with a rule for measuring signed area in pairs of directions. A symplectic embedding is a map that keeps that rule. The question is when several balls embed this way, without overlap, inside a bigger ball. The first test is volume. The second is Gromov's two-ball obstruction: any two capacities must add to less than the target[2]. In dimension four, other obstructions also matter, so these two tests are not enough there[3]. Siegel and Yao conjectured that in higher dimensions they are enough[4].

Earlier work showed volume suffices in special regimes. Biran showed this for many equal balls in dimension four. Buse and Hind extended it to higher dimensions[5]. Buse, Hind and Opshtein did the same for unequal balls when all are very small[6].

The paper proves the full criterion for n at least 3. Balls of capacities R1 to Rk fit in the open ball of capacity R under two tests. The n-th powers of the capacities must add to less than Rⁿ. Each pair must add to less than R. The paper proves these two tests are exactly right[1]. The key obstacle is that the volume test is only an average over a region. It does not say the leftover area is positive at every point, so the balls cannot simply be stacked[7]. The paper fixes this with a Hamiltonian comparison, a controlled motion from classical mechanics that rearranges the leftover area[8]. It builds its models over a curved surface with a handle, using tools from algebraic geometry. The proof splits into three cases, by whether one capacity is at least half the target and whether n is 3[9].

How sure is this? Lean, a computer proof checker, has formal statements of the full criterion for every n at least 3. It also states the necessity direction alone. So the paper proves this result, as far as the Lean statements match the paper. No specialist review is published.
hypeCheck: Major, with Lean statements of the full criterion. It covers dimension six and up only; dimension four has extra obstructions. No specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A space with a rule that measures signed area in pairs of directions.
A map of one shape into another that keeps the symplectic area rule exactly.
For a ball, π times the square of its ordinary radius.
Placing several shapes inside one larger shape with no overlaps.
Two balls fit symplectically in a ball only if their capacities add to less than the target's.
A motion that follows the equations of classical mechanics for some energy function.
The simple test that the pieces' total volume must be less than the target's volume.

claims.text: For n ≥ 3, closed symplectic 2n-balls of capacities R_i embed disjointly into the interior of a ball of capacity R if and only if the sum of R_iⁿ is less than Rⁿ and R_i + R_j < R.
claims.sourceLine:
the closed standard
symplectic \(2n\)-balls of these capacities embed disjointly into the interior
claims.sourceQuote: We prove that, for all integers \(n\ge3\) and \(k\ge1\) and all positive real capacities \(R_1,\ldots,R_k\), the closed standard symplectic \(2n\)-balls of these capacities embed disjointly into the interior of a ball of capacity \(R>0\) if and only if \[ \sum_{i=1}^k R_i^n<R^n, \qquad R_i+R_j<R\quad(i\ne j). \]
